title: Infosys CEO Says US Immigration Curbs Will Not Raise Costs or Attrition
excerpt: Salil Parekh told investors a majority-local US workforce insulates Infosys from the PERM suspension and H-1B pressure, even as individual green-card cases face delays.
body:
• Infosys CEO Salil Parekh told investors the US immigration crackdown, including the October 8 PERM suspension, will not raise costs or drive attrition at the company.
  • Parekh said a majority of Infosys staff in the United States are already local hires, a shift the company has pursued for several years.
  • Infosys reported $5.1 billion in revenue in the quarter ended September 30, 2026, up 1.5% in constant currency, and large deals totaling $5.2 billion.
  • For Indian IT workers in the US: the PERM suspension blocks new employer-sponsored green-card filings at the affected firms, but existing H-1B visas are not cancelled — check your own case status with your employer's immigration counsel.

Infosys expects its US workforce to remain broadly unaffected by the Trump administration's crackdown on employee immigration programs, Chief Executive Salil Parekh told investors on the company's earnings call last week, according to Channel Dive. Parekh said the company sees no cost impact and no rise in attrition from the restrictions.

"We don't see any real impact on attrition from any of those activities. Neither do we see a cost impact because we already have within the U.S. a mix, where the majority of the people are local hires."

— Salil Parekh, Chief Executive, Infosys

What Washington did on October 8

On October 8, the US Department of Labor suspended Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, HCL Technologies and Capgemini from the Permanent Labor Certification Program, citing multiple federal investigations of IT outsourcing, Channel Dive reported. PERM is the Labor Department certification most employers need before sponsoring a worker for an employment-based green card. The wider suspension covered eight firms in total, also including Wipro, Microsoft and Adobe, according to coverage of Infosys's regulatory filing.

Infosys addressed the move directly in an October 10 regulatory filing. The Bengaluru-headquartered company said it did not anticipate the suspension having a material impact on the organization, welcomed the opportunity to work with the Labor Department and related agencies on their questions, and pointed to its investment in a local US workforce and technology and innovation hubs. Its H-1B staff work under a separate temporary-visa program that the PERM action does not cancel.

Why Infosys says the exposure is limited

The company's argument rests on two facts. First, local hiring: Parekh said the majority of its US employees are local hires, a mix built over several years, so delivery to clients does not depend on moving large numbers of staff from India. Second, volume: Indian IT firms have sharply cut PERM filings in recent years. TCS filed just two PERM applications in US fiscal 2026, down from 513 in 2025 and 1,804 in 2024, while HCL submitted 59 filings in 2026 compared with 323 in 2025, according to industry data cited in coverage of the filing. Former HCL Technologies chief executive Vineet Nayar noted that Indian IT companies accounted for less than 2 percent of PERM certifications last year.

That does not make the suspension painless for individuals. A worker whose green-card case depended on a new or pending PERM filing at a suspended firm faces delay and uncertainty even if the employer's revenue is untouched. Coverage of the October 8 suspension noted that the path to permanent residency is effectively blocked in the near term for affected H-1B holders at those companies.

Earnings behind the comments

Parekh made the remarks while reporting results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Infosys posted $5.1 billion in revenue, up 1.5% year over year in constant currency, revised its fiscal 2027 revenue growth guidance to 1-2% in constant currency, and won large deals totaling $5.2 billion, including one deal worth over $2 billion. AI made up 10.5% of revenue, the company said. Parekh said the AI growth reflected client confidence and the company's positioning as an ecosystem integrator working with frontier model companies.

What to watch

The open questions are duration and scope: how long the PERM suspension lasts, what the federal investigations find, and whether further restrictions reach the H-1B program itself. For now, the largest Indian IT firms are sending the same message in filings and on earnings calls — operations continue, local hiring carries the US business, and the immediate financial impact is limited. Employees with pending green-card cases, rather than shareholders, carry most of the near-term risk.
